g.passage: When the buffet doors opened, the wedding hall in Busan dissolved into a hundred conversations, and Sunja let the noise carry her to a corner table. Joon, her grandson, slid in beside her, tugging at a collar his mother had ironed too stiffly. He was laughing about the cousin who had tripped on the aisle runner, and Sunja laughed too, swatting his wrist for being unkind. Then he drew a creased photograph from his jacket: a young woman in a borrowed hanbok, standing beside a man no one in the family had ever named. Sunja's hand stopped above her plate. Around them the hall went on clapping for the couple, but at the corner table the air had thinned. She studied the face she had once worn and did not reach for the picture. Joon, sensing he had opened something he could not close, set his chopsticks down without a sound. Somewhere a microphone squealed, and the master of ceremonies announced the cake.

g.passage: Who goes to the cinema in Tromso in May, when the sun refuses to set and no one needs the dark? Anders asked himself this as he bought a ticket from a girl reading a magazine. Inside, the theater held eleven people, and one of them was Anneke, who had not come to Mass in three years. She waved with the cheerful ease of someone meeting her dentist at a party, and Anders sat two seats away, pleased by the coincidence. They traded jokes about the stale popcorn. Then Anneke's daughter leaned across her mother's lap. "Why don't we go to church anymore?" she asked. "You said it was because Father Anders moved away." Anneke looked at the blank screen. "Sell it," Yaa says, stirring sugar into his glass,
and laughs, and orders bread for both of us,

the waiter could clear away with the cups.
Ama, he says, my name a coin he flips,
you still owe me for the ticket here.

g.passage: We took the letters to the bridge because the apartment was already full of boxes. Mathis, my sister, read the first one aloud in a mock-theatrical voice, and I applauded each of our mother's complaints about the price of leeks, the neighbor's dog, the rain over the Saone. "Etienne, listen to this one," she would say, and bow before reading. For half an hour it felt like a performance staged for two. Then she opened a letter dated the spring before she was born, and her voice dropped. Our mother had written that she was afraid of staying in Lyon forever, afraid she would never see the sea again. Mathis folded the page along its old crease. I thought of her plane ticket, tucked into the passport in her coat, and of how she had mentioned it to me as if mentioning the weather. Below us the river carried a single plastic bottle past the pillars, turning it slowly, never letting it sink.

I was Moshe, a visitor with a swim cap and nothing to do in Addis Ababa until the pump was fixed. We skimmed jacaranda petals off the salt water while the attendant argued on the telephone. It was faintly comic: two grown men, strangers, fishing for flowers. By the fourth morning I was arriving early. Shamsuddin had brought a second net, newer, its handle wrapped in blue tape, and he passed it to me without a word, as one passes a cup at a table. I found I did not want the pump repaired. g.passage: Anselm cooked by ear. On Thursdays he brought his goulash to the weaving cooperative in Vienna where my mother worked, and the women at the looms would stop their shuttles to ask what he put in it. He always shrugged. When my mother died, I asked him to write the recipe down, partly to test him, partly because I did not yet trust a stepfather to keep anything of hers. He tried. He sat at the kitchen table with a pencil for an hour and produced three lines, one of which said only "enough paprika." I, Liesel, was furious, then puzzled. Then, watching him cook the next Thursday, I began to understand. He tasted, waited, added, tasted again, listening to the pot the way the weavers listened to their looms for a slipped thread. Now I bring the goulash myself. The cooperative has new looms, painted green, that clatter louder than the old ones.

That was the Sunday my aunt's church on 47th Street lost its kitchen to a fire and borrowed the narrow galley of a retired lake freighter that a neighbor had turned into a diner on the South Side. The congregation always served fried catfish after service; Darnell's mosque, it turned out, held its Sunday lunch on the same block, and the fire had displaced them too. One galley, one long steel table. For an hour the two groups ate in careful halves, salt shakers lined up like a border. Then Darnell, who knew half the room by their bus stops, began passing plates across the line, calling people by where they got off: Cottage Grove, Halsted, King Drive. "Kenya, Ashland Avenue, pass the hot sauce," he told me. By dessert the halves had blurred. I still take his route, though I sit nearer the front now. Through the windows, the lake looks gray most mornings, then suddenly green.

g.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 어느 쪽의 말도 누그러뜨리지 않는다는 통역사의 원칙을 밝힌다. 앞에서 화자는 이발사와 Dario의 말을 그대로 옮기고, 뒤에서는 이 원칙 때문에 옆 손님이 속삭인 이발사 아들의 사연을 Dario에게 전하지 않는다. 따라서 원칙이 무엇을 빼고 전할지의 결정을 틀 짓는다는 D가 정답이다. A의 방해, B의 이발소 관습 소개, C의 후회는 밑줄 문장의 기능과 맞지 않다.

seed.relationship: a landlord and a long-term tenant
seed.topicSeed: an apartment stairwell in Naples; a landlord and a long-term tenant about leaving versus staying loyal

g.passage: Who counts the steps of a stairwell after forty years? Katarzyna did, every evening, one hundred and twelve from the street door to her landing in the old building in Naples, and the number had never once changed. Lakshmi, who had inherited the building from her father, met her on the third floor with an envelope. The rent was going up; a hotel group had made an offer for the whole block. Lakshmi had lain awake rehearsing this and still delivered it badly, apologizing in the wrong places. Katarzyna had expected it for a year and had prepared nothing at all, so she listened with her hand on the rail, polished pale by her own palm. Each woman, in her way, was trying to be decent about something neither had chosen. When Katarzyna finally took the envelope, she thanked Lakshmi for bringing it in person, which was more than her father had ever done. Then she climbed the remaining steps, counting aloud.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Lakshmi and Katarzyna?
options: Openly critical of Lakshmi for selling the building and dismissive of Katarzyna's attachment
Amused by both women's habits and doubtful that either understands the offer being made
Admiring of Katarzyna's defiance and contemptuous of Lakshmi's attempts to apologize
Sympathetic toward both, presenting each woman's difficulty without taking a side
g.explanation: 서술자는 밤새 연습하고도 서툴게 사과하는 Lakshmi의 불안과, 1년간 예상했지만 아무 준비도 못 한 Katarzyna의 처지를 나란히 같은 비중으로 그린다. 또 두 사람 모두 원치 않은 일에 품위를 지키려 한다고 서술하고, Katarzyna가 직접 와 준 Lakshmi에게 고마워하는 장면으로 어느 편도 들지 않는다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A와 C는 한쪽을 비난하는 태도이고, B는 두 사람이 상황을 이해하지 못한다는 근거가 없다.

g.passage: A smell of rosin and radiator dust hung in the music room after school, where Mabel waited for her stepdaughter to finish practicing. For four months Harriet had spoken to her only in logistics: rides, money, a form to sign. Mabel had stopped trying clever openings. She sat on a folding chair by the timpani, pretending with the conviction of a bad actor to grade quizzes she had already graded twice. Harriet played the same eight bars of a sonata, missed the same note, and played them again. On the ninth try she stopped. "You can say it's bad," she said, without turning around. Mabel considered several answers, each more careful than the last, and gave none of them. "It's the F," she said. "Your mother used to miss it too." Harriet's bow hovered. Then she played the bars once more and, deliberately, missed the F again. Snow ticked against the tall windows, and the radiator knocked twice like a latecomer.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Mabel?
options: Gently amused by her awkwardness yet sympathetic to her patient effort to reach Harriet
Harshly critical of her dishonesty and convinced that she has damaged the family further
Coolly detached from her feelings and interested mainly in the technical details of music
Openly mocking of her musical ignorance and impatient with her reluctance to speak plainly
g.explanation: 서술자는 이미 두 번 채점한 시험지를 '서툰 배우처럼' 채점하는 척하는 Mabel을 가볍게 놀리듯 묘사한다. 그러나 넉 달간 사무적인 말만 들으면서도 영리한 말 걸기를 그만두고 조심스러운 답 대신 진솔한 한마디를 고르는 모습을 공감 어린 시선으로 따라간다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B와 D는 지나치게 적대적이고, C는 Mabel의 내면을 세밀히 그리는 서술과 맞지 않다.

g.passage: We had planned the surprise for weeks: on the last night shift before the clinic closed for renovation, Yona and Xinyi would carry the old break-room table out to the hillside terrace so the three of us could watch the sun come up over the plateau. Yona borrowed a truck with the gravity she gives a medication count; Xinyi, who never forgets anything, brought a thermos and three folding chairs. Everything worked. The sky went orange on schedule, and a hawk crossed it as though hired. And yet we sat there saying very little. Yona kept checking her phone for messages from the day staff. Xinyi rubbed at a coffee ring on the table, a stain from some forgotten night years before. I do not blame them, or myself. I have come to think a good plan can arrange the scenery but not the feeling, and that the arranging was its own kind of kindness. On the drive down, the truck's radio found a station playing fiddle music, then lost it in the canyon.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Yona and Xinyi?

Affectionate and appreciative of their care, even though the outing did not lift their mood

Envious of their friendship and resentful at being left out of the planning for the morning

g.passage: Jamal ran the only all-night pharmacy in our corner of the Delta, and for most of my teens I worked the counter beside him from ten until dawn. We had an agreement, never spoken, that we would not talk about my mother's leaving. Instead we talked about insulin prices, cotton futures, the trucker who bought antacid every Tuesday. I used to think this was cowardice, his and mine. I was Devon then, sixteen and certain I knew everything. Now, writing it down, I see how carefully he built those nights: the radio always tuned to the blues station she liked, her old stool kept behind the register though no one sat on it, the coffee made too strong, the way she made it. He was not avoiding her. He was keeping a room for her and letting me stay in it with him. Outside, the crop dusters started at five, low over the fields, their engines like a second dawn.
g.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward his father in the text?
options: Lingering resentment at his father's refusal ever to discuss the mother's departure
Amused indifference toward his father's habits, which he regards as harmless quirks
A revised, tender understanding of silences he once judged as mere avoidance
Sharp disapproval of his father for running a business that kept his son up all night
g.explanation: 화자는 예전에는 어머니 이야기를 피하는 침묵을 비겁함이라 여겼다고 말한다. 그러나 지금은 어머니가 좋아하던 라디오 채널, 비워 둔 의자, 진한 커피를 떠올리며 아버지가 그녀를 위한 자리를 지키고 있었다고 다시 이해한다. 따라서 과거의 판단을 고친 다정한 이해라는 C가 정답이다. A의 원망은 과거의 생각일 뿐이고, B의 무관심과 D의 비난은 지문과 맞지 않다.

g.passage: Wrapping paper crackled under Vesna's fingers as she slid the package across the diner table outside Riga, where the orchestra bus had stopped for soup. Inside was a wool scarf in a vivid mustard yellow, the one color Zofia had told the whole string section she could not bear. The conductor held it up and declared it perfect. She wore it through lunch, through the second half of the drive, and onto the stage that night, where it clashed magnificently with the black of the orchestra. Vesna, the youngest player, watched from the last desk with her face burning, half proud and half mortified. Afterward, in the corridor, Zofia folded the scarf carefully and told the stage manager it had kept her warm all evening. Outside, the bus idled in the snow, coughing gray clouds under the parking lot's single streetlamp.
g.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray how a conductor's sustained pretense spares the feelings of a young musician

g.passage: Ink and machine oil were the first smells I learned in the printing room in Chiang Mai, and the third, after a month, was the steam from Kiet's iron. She rented the back corner from the press owner and sewed there with her only apprentice, Zhiming, between the stacks of temple calendars. In my first week I watched Zhiming hand Kiet every pin before she asked for it. By spring Kiet's eyes had begun to fail, and the roles reversed in small ways neither mentioned: Zhiming threaded the needles now, read the measurements aloud, and left the cutting chalk exactly where Kiet's hand would fall. Kiet still announced each morning's work as if she had planned it. Zhiming still said, "Yes, teacher." The press thundered on beside them, turning out invitations for weddings I would never attend, their gold lettering drying in rows along the windowsill.
g.question: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how the narrator first came to work in a busy printing room in Chiang Mai
To depict how an apprentice quietly shields her teacher's dignity as their roles reverse
To explain how a printing press produces calendars and wedding invitations for temples
To argue that every skilled craft must eventually be handed down to a younger generation
g.explanation: 처음에는 Zhiming이 Kiet가 요청하기 전에 핀을 건네는 보조 역할을 한다. 봄이 되어 Kiet의 시력이 약해지자 실제로는 Zhiming이 바늘에 실을 꿰고 치수를 읽어 주지만, Kiet는 여전히 작업을 지시하고 Zhiming은 '네, 선생님'이라고 답하며 겉모습을 유지한다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 도입 일화만 요약했고, C는 소재는 같지만 목적이 다르며, D는 지나치게 일반적인 교훈이다.
